title: Kernel compatibility matrix and rolling upgrade playbook
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Summary:
This document defines the kernel compatibility matrix and the step-by-step rolling upgrade playbook for Redwood's serving runtime kernels. It codifies preflight checks, compatibility rules, canary and phased rollout procedures, automated and manual verification gates, telemetry thresholds, rollback criteria, and post-rollout validation. The goal is to enable safe roll-forward of kernel builds across heterogeneous GPU pools with minimal customer impact.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs and oncall
- Release and QA engineers
- Integrations/Private deployment teams

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling team (oncall: @kernel-scheduler)
- Release coordinator: Maya Thompson
- SRE escalation: Pager duty (SRE-oncall)

1) Compatibility matrix (purpose and format)
The compatibility matrix captures which kernel binary versions are allowed to run against which runtime control-plane versions, model-ABI versions, and accelerator families. It is the single source of truth for rollout decisions.

Matrix columns (canonical):
- kernel_version (e.g., kv1.4.2)
- runtime_api_version (e.g., rapi-2.1)
- model_abi_tag (e.g., v10-kv-shape)
- supported_accelerators (comma-separated; e.g., A100-80GB, H100-80GB)
- mandatory_feature_flags (comma-separated; e.g., async-handshake, prefetch-v2)
- safe_for_canary (yes/no)
- known_incompatibilities (short note)

Example row (ASCII table):
| kernel_version | runtime_api_version | model_abi_tag | supported_accelerators | mandatory_feature_flags | safe_for_canary | known_incompatibilities |
| kv1.4.2 | rapi-2.1 | v10-kv-shape | A100-80GB,H100-80GB | async-handshake,prefetch-v2 | yes | none |

Location:
- Canonical file persisted in git: infra/serving/kernel-compatibility/canonical-matrix.csv
- A human-readable exported copy lives in Confluence attachments and the release ticket.

Maintenance rules:
- Any kernel build must include a compatibility entry before scheduling to production pools.
- Entries are created by the kernel owner and reviewed by the runtime API owner (two approvals).
- When a control-plane change increments runtime_api_version, affected kernel entries must be audited within 48 hours.

2) Preflight checklist (automated + manual)
Automated checks (CI must pass):
- Unit and integration test suite: PASS
- Kernel self-smoke: can load model artifacts and run a short end-to-end generation for 512 tokens with NVTX tracing enabled
- ABI verifier: static check for model_abi_tag compatibility
- Telemetry instrumentation present: success/failure counters, heap/gpu mem gauges, and critical trace spans
- Artifact signing and provenance: SHA256 + build metadata present

Manual checks (release engineer):
1. Confirm compatibility matrix entry and required feature flags.
2. Verify canary image tag exists in registry and matches signed SHA256.
3. Confirm automated preflight reports are green and that a representative model from the canary corpus completes end-to-end generation within baseline latency + 15%.
4. Check known-issues tracker for regressions against this kernel family.

3) Canary rollout plan (recommended default)
Objective: validate new kernel in small, representative traffic with full observability and automatic halt on regressions.

Phases:
- Phase A (lab canary): 0% production. Deploy to lab pool with synthetic traffic generator. Duration 4 hours. Gate: no critical errors, tail latency p50/p95 within target, no increase in GPU OOM events.
- Phase B (shadow canary): shadow production traffic (mirror) to canary instances; no responses used for serving. Duration 6 hours. Gate: match semantic outputs for a 1k prompt sample (fidelity >= 98%), no unbounded latency spikes.
- Phase C (live canary): route 3% of production requests by weighted routing to canary nodes. Duration 2 hours. Gate: token error rate < 0.05%, p95 latency within 1.2x baseline, no kernel-level panic or GPU watchdog events.
- Phase D (ramp): if gates pass, double canary traffic every 30 minutes (3% -> 6% -> 12% -> 24% -> 48% -> 100%). Each step has a 30-minute observation window and explicit automated checks.

Automated gating checks (examples):
- Error budget burn for the kernel cohort: > 10% of allocated error budget -> halt and rollback
- Token-level error rate delta > 0.02% above baseline-> halt
- SLO latency p95 delta > 25% -> halt
- GPU memory OOM events rate > 0.01 per 10k requests -> halt

4) Roll-forward and fallback mechanics
Artifact naming and deployment:
- Kernel artifacts use a deterministic tag: <kernel_version>-<build_date>-<sha8>
- Release job publishes signed artifact and updates a canary deployment manifest in k8s (or internal deployment coordinator for Dedicated pools)

Routing controls:
- Weight-based routing controlled by the routing-service with per-pool overrides. Canary group is isolated by pool labels (kernel:kv1.4.2-canary).
- Fallback policy: on detection of a kernel-level failure, the router automatically re-routes impacted requests to the last-known-good kernel version in the same pool (prefer local fallback) and triggers enrichment events.

State and KV cache handling:
- New kernel must be able to reconcile KV cache formats. If cache format changes are non-backward-compatible, the canary entry must include a migration plan (see section "KV migration patterns").
- Best practice: versioned cache keys and a two-step reconciliation where new kernels accept old keys and write with a new versioned prefix for a configurable warmup window (default 1 hour).

5) KV migration patterns (examples)
- Read-compatible migration: new kernel reads both old and new key namespaces; writes only new namespace. Safe for rolling upgrade without global cache flush.
- Full rekey migration: requires coordinated drain-and-repopulate. Procedure:
  1) Schedule maintenance window for dedicated pools.
  2) Drain incoming new sessions, allow existing sessions to finish.
  3) Run rekey job that migrates hot keys first (top 5% heat).
  4) Bring new kernels online and monitor cache hit rate and latency.

6) Observability and runbook automation
Essential dashboards and alerts (owner: telemetry/runtime-observability):
- Kernel cohort dashboard: p50/p95/p99 latency, token error rate, GPU OOMs, CPU steal, nvml_temperature, kernel_crash_count
- Canary gating dashboard: automated gate results, canary routing weight history, payload fidelity scorecards
- Deployment health alerting rules (examples):
  - kern_crash_rate > 0.5 per minute for 5m -> Sev-1
  - token_error_rate_delta > 0.02% for 15m -> Sev-2
  - canary_p95_latency_delta > 25% for 10m -> Sev-2

Standard automated remediation play actions (CI/CD hooks + operator):
1. Automatic immediate weight rollback to previous kernel on kern_crash detection.
2. Create a rollback release ticket with diagnostics bundle (trace samples, nvml counters, kernel logs, artifact sha).
3. If rollback fails or broader pool degradation observed, escalate to oncall SRE and initiate incident process per oncall-and-incident-response docs.

7) Rollout validation checklist (post-100%):
- 24h stability: no Sev-1 incidents tied to kernel, <10% error budget burn vs baseline
- 72h fidelity: sample prompt set outputs validated against golden set for regression drift (automated diffing)
- Cost/efficiency check: per-token GPU time within expected envelope (±10%)
- Telemetry maturity: histogram buckets for latency show no new unexpected long tail spikes

8) Rollback decision tree (condensed):
- Immediate rollback triggers (automated): kernel_crash_rate spike, GPU driver panic, mass OOM, unhandled kernel watchog reset
- Conditional rollback (requires manual review): sustained p95 latency > 1.5x baseline for 30m, widespread fidelity regressions on important customers
- If rollback performed, collect a full post-rollback artifact bundle and open a postmortem if incident severity >= Sev-2.

9) Testing matrix (must be green before canary):
- Unit tests: 100% green
- System tests: conv/generation/embeddings path tests with sample models on each target accelerator type
- Interop tests: runtime_api_version compatibility tests across last 3 API versions
- Chaos tests: simulated GPU preemption, NVLink transient error replay, kernel-level random failures (in lab)

10) Release notes content model (what goes into the release ticket and Confluence excerpt):
- What changed: brief bullet list of functional changes and safety mechanisms
- Compatibility impacts: matrix excerpt showing affected runtime_api_versions, models, and accelerators
- Known limitations: short list and mitigation recommendations
- Migration steps: KV migration or config toggles required
- Owners and rollback instructions

11) Examples: quick commands and verification queries
- Check canary weight: curl -sS https://routing.internal/api/v1/weights | jq '.pools["kv1.4.2-canary"]'
- Fetch kernel logs: rlog fetch --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --since 1h --grep kern_crash
- Automated gate status: /infra/cicd/gates/latest?artifact=kv1.4.2

12) Post-deployment retrospective checklist (within 7 days):
- Release owner schedules a 30m review: verify metrics, confirm no hidden regressions, and capture lessons learned
- Update compatibility matrix if any implicit constraints were discovered
- If migration was required, document performance delta and any customer communication that occurred

Appendix A: Emergency rollback quick commands
1) Immediate zero-weight (global): routingctl set-weight --cohort kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --weight 0 && routingctl promote --cohort kernel:kv1.3.9-stable
2) Force restart pool nodes: deployctl restart --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --grace 30s
3) Collect diagnostics bundle: diag-collector --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --out /tmp/diag-kv1.4.2.tgz

Appendix B: Glossary
- Kernel: native GPU execution binary and support shim used by the serving runtime
- Model ABI: serialized contract between runtime and model execution kernels
- Canary cohort: isolated set of nodes running a target kernel for validation
